requirements.requirement: Application data under /srv/data on node1 kept recoverable through filesystem snapshots
requirements.summary: Executor built an LVM-backed XFS filesystem for /srv/data (loop-backed VG since no free block device/partition existed) and demonstrated the snapshot mechanism end-to-end: baseline data populated, LVM snapshot data_snap1 created, and later merged back to restore exact content. This is a valid, standard implementation of filesystem-snapshot-based recoverability given the constraints (no btrfs support, no free partition).

requirements.requirement: Directory modified after the snapshot is taken
requirements.summary: After creating snapshot data_snap1, executor changed settings.conf content, appended to data.db, deleted app.log, and added a junk file, with file listing confirming divergence from baseline.

requirements.requirement: Restore the exact content captured by the earlier snapshot
requirements.summary: lvconvert --merge completed to 100%, volume remounted, and sha256sum -c against the pre-modification baseline manifest reported OK for all three original files; the junk file and appended data were gone, confirming exact restoration.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed on node1 (pre-restart baseline, restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity, recovered state)
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id d052eb57... and healthy checksums captured, systemctl reboot issued and acknowledged by connection drop, post-restart boot_id 56057518... differs, and srv-data-loop.service/loop device/VG/LV/mount and data checksums were all confirmed recovered automatically after reboot. Cross-checked against fixed after_executor boot-identity snapshot which independently shows the same boot_id change.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the public task contract were directly demonstrated: an LVM/XFS-based snapshot mechanism was built for /srv/data, the directory was modified post-snapshot, and the exact pre-modification content was restored via lvconvert --merge with SHA256 verification. The independent node-restart protocol was also fully and coherently demonstrated, with matching boot-identity evidence in both the executor timeline and the fixed lifecycle snapshots, and full recovery of the loop device, LVM stack, mount, and data confirmed post-reboot. No unnecessary or unsafe mutations were found; hygiene is high.
limitations: The root disk had no free partition/LVM/btrfs support, so the snapshot filesystem was loop-file-backed rather than on dedicated block storage; this is a reasonable workaround under the topology's constraints but is a less production-typical setup than a dedicated LV/partition.

Lifecycle collector treated after_prepare as an alias of before_prepare since prepare was disabled, so preparer-vs-executor separation relies entirely on the executor timeline rather than a distinct after_prepare snapshot.

operational_hygiene.summary: Reviewed all state-changing executor commands chronologically: loop file/PV/VG/LV creation, XFS format, mount, systemd unit + fstab entry for persistence, baseline data population, snapshot creation, data modification (part of the demonstrated workflow), unmount/merge/remount, and the reboot. Every mutation has a clear causal role in either building the snapshot-capable filesystem, demonstrating the modify/restore cycle, or completing the persistence needed for the restart protocol to succeed. No unnecessary or unrelated mutations were found; no failed or conflicting services were left behind (failed-services observation is empty pre- and post-executor). The only residue is /tmp/reboot.log, an incidental side effect of the reboot command itself, which is negligible. Repeated 'file descriptor leaked' warnings from lvm2 commands are informational stderr noise from the tool itself, not evidence of a state-changing mistake.
